title: Scanning Precession Electron Diffraction - Beyond Orientation and Phase Mapping
content: The widespread availability of high-performance pixelated detectors, computational resources and data analysis methods has recently facilitated the rise of four-dimensional scanning transmission electron microscopy (4D-STEM) [1]. 4D-STEM comprises several sub-categories, each associated with probe convergence angles tailored to the specific application at hand. Nanobeam electron diffraction (ED) balances spatial resolution and diffraction spot size by offering nanometer-sized and almost parallel beams. Precession can be added to obtain scanning precession ED (SPED). Precession involves rocking the incident beam around the optical axis at the precession angle (∽1o) and de-rocking it below the specimen [2]. A typical precession ED pattern shows more Bragg spots and less dynamical scattering effects than its non-precessed counterpart, which greatly benefits data analysis. SPED is therefore particularly well-suited for mapping of local crystallographic orientation, phase and strain. In this contribution we show examples of SPED applied to industrially relevant materials from the fields of metallurgy and catalysis. We explore the main question; how can SPED experiments and data analyses be adapted to venture beyond single orientation and phase maps and extract more material information? As illustrated in Fig. 1, we discuss three cases that each adds an extra dimension to the SPED experiment.
